segments.text: Over fifteen billion miles away, Voyager One was sending signals nobody could read.
The trouble began in November twenty twenty-three: a failed memory chip in its data-packaging computer.
Engineers couldn't repair the chip. So they moved the affected code.
But it wouldn't fit in one place.
They split it across working memory, then updated the instructions so the pieces still worked together.
A command took about twenty-two and a half hours just to reach the spacecraft.
On April twentieth, twenty twenty-four, readable engineering data came back. Science data followed later.
The chip stayed broken. The software worked around it.

misconceptionSafeguards: Radio signal continued; unreadable data is not silence.
Code moves, hardware does not. Failed chip remains red/disabled throughout.
Memory slots and instruction tiles are qualitative; not real Voyager software, literal addresses or measured capacity.
April20engineering data is separate from later science recovery.
Distance and light time explicitly historical April2024.
No physical chip repair, astronaut intervention, unsupported failure cause or present-day health claim.
review.comprehensionReview: Concrete vocabulary: code represented as instructions; no addresses, machine language or programming prerequisite. A failed fit motivates splitting. Connecting separate pieces explains reference updates. Dated return is the promised payoff.
review.rightsReview: NASA/JPL concept imagery credited and labeled artist concept; no identifiable people or logos. JPL image-use policy inspected, exact image pages and downloads retained. Original graphics/sound; existing licensed fonts and local Kokoro.
